summary: Several other MVA-associated BUBR1 missense mutants had reduced protein abundance and increased turnover. This supports investigating residual-protein stabilization, not instability of the hypothetical alleles or activity of either mapped drug.
HSP90 inhibition with geldanamycin reduced I909T and L1012P mutant BUBR1 abundance in cells. Loss under inhibition is not evidence that arimoclomol or HSP70 induction stabilizes BUBR1.

Forced expression of I909T and L1012P to levels comparable to wild-type restored the nocodazole checkpoint response in a replacement-cell assay. This was genetic expression manipulation, not treatment with either mapped drug and not exact-variant rescue.

The stable Y155C mutant restored chromosome alignment but not checkpoint activity in the studied assay. Protein abundance alone therefore cannot establish functional correction of a different BUBR1 allele.

Transcript and protein findings for other BUBR1 truncations were consistent with transcript loss and possible nonsense-mediated decay. This motivates measuring transcript availability before any readthrough experiment; it is not gentamicin evidence or proof of decay for the hypothetical allele.

Figure 6 reports arimoclomol treatment of NPC patient fibroblasts and NPC-model mice: reduced fibroblast lysosomal storage and cholesterol accumulation, and increased brain HSF1 activation and HSP70 in treated mice. This is primary drug-tested evidence in another disease, not BUBR1 stabilization, MVA efficacy or exact-variant rescue.

Section 1 lists MIPLYFFA with miglustat for neurological manifestations of NPC in adults and pediatric patients aged 2 years and older. This establishes approved-product eligibility only, not numeric translation evidence, approval or efficacy for MVA.
Section 12.1 states that the mechanism of arimoclomol's clinical effects in NPC is unknown. Regulatory approval does not validate the proposed BUBR1 chaperone mechanism.

Sections 8.6 and 12.3 describe increased arimoclomol exposure with moderate to severe renal impairment and an unevaluated lowest-renal-function category. These are labeled population constraints, not evidence of renal impairment in the hypothetical case.

Sections 5.3, 7.1 and 12.3 describe reversible creatinine increases without measured glomerular-function change, OCT2 inhibition and possible increased exposure of OCT2 substrates. Creatinine changes should not automatically be equated with kidney injury.

Section 6.1 reports decreased weight, decreased appetite and diarrhea in the subgroup also receiving miglustat, and hypersensitivity reactions in the trial. Combination-population observations cannot be assigned solely to arimoclomol or assumed to occur in MVA.

Cell and biochemical experiments linked SIRT2-dependent deacetylation of BubR1 lysine 668 to reduced ubiquitylation and increased stability. This supplies pathway rationale, not niacin treatment evidence or correction of a specific BUB1B variant.

NMN treatment increased BubR1 abundance in wild-type mice. The paper's lifespan experiment used SIRT2 overexpression in hypomorphic mice, not niacin or NMN treatment; neither result establishes niacin-mediated checkpoint rescue.

Nicotinamide used as a sirtuin inhibitor reduced BubR1 levels in the reported cell experiments. This is a compound-and-context caution against treating nicotinic acid, nicotinamide and NMN as interchangeable, not proof that niacin harms BUBR1 function.

The primary study abstract reports that administered niacin increased blood NAD in adult-onset mitochondrial-myopathy patients and matched controls, with patient muscle NAD reaching control levels. This establishes human pharmacodynamic observations in a different disease, not NAD deficiency, muscle benefit, BUBR1 correction or feasible exposure in the hypothetical MVA case.

Sections 11 and 12.3 identify the product as nicotinic acid and describe a metabolic pathway producing NAD. This biochemical entry point does not establish a target-tissue NAD increase, SIRT2 engagement or BUBR1 rescue in MVA.

Section 1 lists lipid-disorder indications for prescription extended-release niacin. This is approved-product eligibility only, not numeric translation evidence, MVA treatment evidence or interchangeability with supplements or other formulations.

Sections 4 and 8.4-8.7 state that safety and effectiveness at age 16 years or younger are unestablished, advise renal caution, and list active liver disease and specified unexplained hepatic abnormalities as contraindications. No individual contraindication is inferred without relevant clinical data.

Section 5.2 describes rhabdomyolysis associated with concomitant niacin and statins. This is a medication-review constraint, not evidence of statin exposure or drug-induced muscle injury in the hypothetical case.

The boxed warning describes nephrotoxicity, potentially irreversible auditory or vestibular toxicity, and added concern with other nephrotoxic or ototoxic drugs. These labeled hazards inform research triage but do not prove a case-specific contraindication.
